name: Hassan Rahman

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time, Hassan. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. Everything you tell me is confidential, so you can say what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. To start, could you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm at a tiny studio, three of us, in an old print works by the canal. We make social media ads, logos and posters for gyms, barbers, a climbing wall, that kind of client. I use AI tools all day: I'll generate twenty rough directions for a gym's summer campaign before lunch, then pick two and actually design them properly. I share a flat with my mate Dmitri, who's a chef.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What do you like most about the work, and what wears you out?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I love the speed now. A client brief that used to take three days of sketching takes an afternoon, and I get to spend the rest on the bit that's actually mine. What wears me out is that the pay hasn't moved with it. I'm doing more for the same low wage, and I've got maybe three weeks of rent in the bank.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. Here's the card: "Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's a decent tool and people overhyped it, both ways. Online I'd post a few of my workflows, because people ask. Nothing dramatic.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd be a bit disappointed, honestly. I've bet some of my identity on being the guy who's good with these tools. But the real issue is still my wage, which is low, and the fact there are only two studios in town.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep going as I am and ask Sam, my boss, for a pay rise based on how much faster I'm working. I'd do a couple of freelance logo jobs on weekends for extra money. I'd want two months of rent saved by next winter.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy. Not about the robots, about the rent and the fact I've got no room to fail.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you're faster. Has that turned into more money for you or for the studio?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: For the studio, completely. We take on more clients at the same price, and I get the same pay. That annoys me more than any AI headline does.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If Sam says no to the raise, then what?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Then I'd keep freelancing on the side and start looking at studios in the city. It's an hour on the train. I'd rather not move, but I can't stay on this money forever.

say: I'd say AI is a **decent tool** that people overhyped both ways.
I'd post my **workflows** online, because people ask for them.
think: Privately, I'd be **disappointed**, because I've built my identity on these tools.
The real issue is my **low wage** and only **two studios** in town.
do: Ask Sam (my boss) for a **pay rise** based on my speed.
Take **weekend freelance** logo jobs for extra money.
Save **two months** of rent by next winter.
feel: **Uneasy** about the rent and having **no room** to fail.
S0.quote: We take on more clients at the same price, and I get the same pay. That annoys me more than any AI headline does.
fieldNote: Hassan already uses AI daily, and his complaint is that the **gains** go to the studio.
His worry in this picture is **pay and rent**, not technology.
He'd look at **city studios** an hour away if a raise doesn't come.

steps.text: Ask Sam for a raise based on faster turnaround
Take weekend freelance logo jobs for local businesses
Save two months of rent by next winter

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. Here's the card: "Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say the tools are here, so let's make sure workers share the gains. I'd post about designers forming co-ops, owning the studio together. I'd tell younger designers to learn the tools but also to organise.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I think I'm one of the last people the studio would cut, because I'm the one running the tools. But that's cold comfort. If the studio drops from three to two, my friend Kasia, the other designer, is the one who goes, and I'd be doing her work too.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd sit down with Kasia and two freelancers I know and plan a small co-op studio, where we split the profit. I'd put three evenings a week into learning motion design and 3D, which the tools still struggle to make feel right. I'd join the union, mainly to push for a rule that AI savings get shared.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but almost excited too. That's a strange mix to admit.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Starting a co-op with less than a month saved sounds risky. How would you fund it?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No office, no loan. We'd work from our flats and a shared online board, and only pay ourselves from jobs that come in. If it fails, I'd still have the studio job for a while.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who would your clients be?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The same kind, gyms, barbers, small shops, but also the people who start using AI themselves and get a mess. A lot of small shops will need someone to fix what the app made. I'd be that person.

say: I'd say workers must **share the gains** from the tools.
I'd post about designers forming **co-ops** and owning their studios.
think: I'm one of the last to be cut, because I **run the tools**.
If the studio shrinks, Kasia goes and I'd be doing **her work** too.
do: Plan a **co-op studio** with Kasia and two freelancers.
Learn **motion design** and **3D** three evenings a week.
Join the union to push for **shared savings**.
feel: **Anxious**, with an **excitement** he finds strange to admit.
S1.quote: A lot of small shops will need someone to fix what the app made. I'd be that person.
fieldNote: Hassan sees himself as **safe for now**, but worries about his colleague Kasia.
His answer to disruption is **ownership**, through a low-cost co-op studio.
He spots a market in **fixing** clients' own AI designs.

steps.text: Start a co-op studio with Kasia and two freelancers, working from home
Learn motion design and 3D three evenings a week
Join the union to push for sharing AI savings with staff

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. Here's the card: "Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is the moment for a basic income and for taxing the AI companies, and I'd mean it. I'd be organising, not just posting. At work I'd tell everyone straight that we've got about a year.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, being good with the tools doesn't save me if the tools can do the whole job. Design is screen work start to finish, so it goes on the AGI date, not three years later with the robots. My edge disappears the day anyone can just ask the machine.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: First month, I'd stop the 3D course, because that's thinking work too. I'd ask Dmitri to get me shifts in his kitchen, because cooking is hands-on and that buys three years. And I'd help set up a local group pushing the council for an emergency support fund.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed. I'm used to being ahead with AI, and AGI by 2028 is the first picture where being ahead doesn't help.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Cooking is quite a change. Are you serious about the kitchen?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Half serious. I can cook, I've helped Dmitri on busy Saturdays. It would be about rent, not a dream, and I'd hate the burns. But a kitchen still needs hands until about 2031.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What happens to the co-op idea in this picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It probably dies before it starts. Clients wouldn't pay us for what they can get free. Maybe we'd do one last thing together, like a campaign for the support fund.

say: I'd call for a **basic income** and **taxing AI** companies.
I'd tell colleagues straight that we have **about a year**.
think: Being good with the tools doesn't help when they do the **whole job**.
Design is **screen work**, so it goes on the AGI date.
do: Drop the **3D course**, since it's thinking work too.
Ask Dmitri for **kitchen shifts** to buy three years.
Set up a local group pushing for an **emergency fund**.
feel: **Alarmed**, because being **ahead** stops helping for the first time.
S2.quote: I'm used to being ahead with AI, and AGI by 2028 is the first picture where being ahead doesn't help.
fieldNote: Hassan's early adoption **stops protecting** him once AI does whole jobs.
He would move to **hands-on kitchen work** to buy about three years.
He shifts from **personal plans** to organising a local group.

steps.text: Take kitchen shifts at Dmitri's restaurant to cover rent
Set up a local group of laid-off creative workers
Push the council for an emergency support fund

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. Here's the card: "Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is long enough to build something fair, if we start now. I'd push the co-op idea hard, and push the union for a deal with employers. Online I'd share what I'm learning, openly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, this one feels like a race I could win for a few years. I'd make good money helping businesses switch to AI before it does everything. After 2031, I'd need to be somewhere else.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd launch the co-op properly in the first year, selling setup work: helping small shops use the AI tools for their own posts. I'd put every extra bit of income into savings until I have three months. And I'd start thinking about a people-facing job for after, maybe running training workshops.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but in a busy way. I'd be working flat out.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: There's a contradiction there. You'd be helping the change happen that ends your job. How do you feel about that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Yeah, I've thought about it. I'd rather small shops and workers get the benefit than just the big companies. If AI is coming anyway, I want it to land in our town's hands, not just the big companies'.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you do in 2031 itself?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Close the design side and keep whatever is about people, training, community work. And hope the government has done something by then, because I won't have a fortune.

say: I'd say five years is enough to build **something fair** if we start now.
I'd push the **co-op** and a union deal with employers.
think: This feels like a **race** I could win for a few years.
After **2031**, I'd need to be somewhere else.
do: Launch the co-op selling **AI setup help** to small shops.
Save every extra bit until I have **three months**.
Plan a **people-facing** job, like running workshops.
S3.quote: If AI is coming anyway, I want it to land in our town's hands, not just the big companies'.
fieldNote: Hassan sees **short-term money** in helping small firms adopt AI.
He accepts the **contradiction** of speeding up the change that ends his job.
He plans to keep only **people work** after 2031.

steps.text: Launch the co-op selling AI setup help to local shops

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last picture is called AGI by 2036. Here's the card: "Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we have a decade, so let's use it to make sure the gains are shared. I'd keep the co-op and union work going. Mostly I'd be calm in public.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, ten years is plenty for me. I'd be thirty-seven, with years of experience helping businesses adapt. I think I'd move into training or running a community studio well before the end point.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: This year I'd do what I'm doing: use the tools, freelance, save. I'd start the co-op slowly, maybe one client a month. And I'd take a short course in teaching adults, so I can run workshops later.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, I'd say. It's on my mind, but I've got time and I like change.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Does ten years change anything personal for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Probably whether I move to the city. With ten years I'd stay here, near my family, and build something local. With two years, I'd go wherever the work was.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would still bother you in this picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That most people around me won't use the ten years well. My mum's friends, the guys at the barbers. I'd want the council doing free classes, not leaving it to people like me.

say: I'd say a decade gives time to make sure **gains are shared**.
I'd stay **calm in public** and keep the co-op going.
think: Ten years is **plenty** for me at **thirty-seven**.
I'd move into **training** or a community studio before the end.
do: Keep using the tools, **freelancing** and saving.
Grow the co-op slowly, about **one client a month**.
Take a short course in **teaching adults**.
feel: **Uneasy**, but with **time** and a taste for change.
S4.quote: With ten years I'd stay here, near my family, and build something local. With two years, I'd go wherever the work was.
fieldNote: Hassan's mood rises and falls with **time**, more than with the end point.
He'd stay **near family** with a decade, but move with only two years.
He worries more about **neighbours** who won't adapt than about himself.

steps.text: Keep freelancing and saving alongside the studio job
Grow the co-op by about one client a month

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028. Being quick doesn't help when there's no time at all. What would help is a basic income or at least a year of support, and real money for people to start co-ops instead of everything going to the big tech firms.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Ask who gets the time saved. In every picture, the question for me isn't whether the tools work. The question is who gets the extra hours and the extra money, and right now it's never the designer.

headlineQuote: The question for me isn't whether the tools work. The question is who gets the extra hours and the extra money, and right now it's never the designer.
portrait: Hassan is a **27-year-old designer** at a three-person studio who uses **AI daily**.
His main complaint is that faster work hasn't raised his **low pay**.
He answers change with **co-ops**, union work and side income, not retreat.
Only in **AGI by 2028** does his early-adopter edge stop helping, pushing him toward kitchen work.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, because being quick doesn't help when there's no time.
whatWouldHelp: A **basic income** or a year of support, plus money for **worker co-ops**.
